pattern: Typed process ports and owned carrier legs

pattern: Hash-linked transcript journal with prepare, commit, abort, recovery, and pinned migration route
current_project_counterpart: MASTER_OPERATING_PROMPT.md durable execution and transcript requirements; R-002 false completion; no selected store
recommended_action: Specify a tenant-scoped append-only conversation/event journal with hash-linked checkpoints, idempotent prepare/commit/abort, immutable route/version ownership, and replay invariants.
acceptance_test: Crash at every persistence boundary; replay must produce the same visible transcript and tool state exactly once, detect conflicting tails, and never roll a conversation back to an older regime.
score_rationale: COR5: checkpoint hashes, file identity, WAL-like pending records, and conflict detection preserve ordering. MOD4: journal and legacy ports are separated, with some file-specific coupling. DUR5: fsync, parent sync, atomic install, prepare/commit/abort, and recovery are explicit. MT2: conversation IDs are not tenant-scoped in the contract. SEC3: tamper/corruption detection is strong, but authorization and encryption are outside the module. MP4: provider-neutral checkpointing. TP4: text and tool envelopes are represented. OBS4: operation outcomes and causes are reported. TST4: deterministic faults can be injected at each boundary, though repository coverage is incomplete. MNT4: versioned records and pinned migration route reduce drift. COST4: incremental append is efficient. PROD5: directly supports reliable visible continuity. SAAS4: strong translation after distributed storage and tenancy are added. GEN5 and FIN5: both need replayable evidence; finance benefits especially from immutable lineage. MIG4: significant event-model and migration work. DEP2: algorithmic pattern is portable.
notes: Do not copy the legacy JSONL envelope; define an independent canonical event schema.

pattern: Content-addressed durable workspace with versioned manifest, conflict handling, and hydration evidence
current_project_counterpart: MASTER_OPERATING_PROMPT.md persistent sandbox, artifacts, recovery, and external-state verification requirements; FILE_MANIFEST.json is a static Stage 0 snapshot
recommended_action: Use immutable blobs plus a versioned tenant/workspace manifest, compare-and-swap canonical commits, explicit hydration completeness, exclusion policy, and readback verification.
acceptance_test: Concurrent writers, partial uploads, oversized objects, metadata loss, restore interruption, and stale manifests must either converge to a verified canonical snapshot or fail closed with retained conflict evidence.
score_rationale: COR4: content identity and canonical conflict readback are strong, but snapshot-out categories and eventual windows can still lose recent work. MOD4: object-store, manifest, transfer, and capture ports are separated. DUR5: append-only blobs, manifests, locks, retries, and hydration markers are comprehensive. MT2: store IDs exist without demonstrated tenant policy or cryptographic tenant binding. SEC3: protected paths and excludes help, but object authorization and encryption are external. MP3: mostly provider-neutral. TP4: preserves workspace and execution artifacts. OBS5: cycle, conflict, capture, byte, and failure summaries are explicit. TST4: deterministic object-store faults are injectable, though end-to-end restore tests were not found in the small public test suite. MNT4: schemas and versions aid evolution. COST3: deduplication helps but snapshots and large-object transfer can be expensive. PROD5: durable workspaces are central to product continuity. SAAS4: useful after tenant isolation and retention are added. GEN5 and FIN5: shared core value is high; finance additionally needs point-in-time data and calculation manifests. MIG5: substantial storage, migration, and operations work. DEP2: storage ports are portable.
notes: Adopt the invariant set, not its local paths, backend names, or snapshot cadence.

current_project_counterpart: MASTER_OPERATING_PROMPT.md Stage 3 compute-isolation alternatives and Stage 4 sandbox/computer spikes

pattern: One owned local Docker container as a production tenant sandbox
current_project_counterpart: No selected compute substrate; R-003, R-004, R-009, R-019 require stronger isolation and scope
recommended_action: Do not use this implementation as the production multi-tenant or untrusted-workload boundary; retain only the idea of a bounded local development provider for a future spike.
acceptance_test: Security test proves no host credential mount, no floating image, resource and syscall confinement, deny-by-default egress, per-job identity, destruction, and cross-tenant isolation; this implementation is not eligible to take that test as production evidence.
score_rationale: COR3: ownership labels, health checks, and content-addressed runtime mounts improve local repeatability, but recreate semantics are coarse. MOD3: settings routing is clear while Docker CLI and product lifecycle are tightly coupled. DUR3: named volumes persist state, but snapshot/RPO guarantees are absent. MT1: one fixed container and volumes have no tenant boundary. SEC1: host CLI credential directories are mounted, gateway binds inside the container, no resource/capability/seccomp/read-only-root/egress policy is set, and a floating image is used. MP3: local provider sessions work. TP4: broad local tools are available. OBS3: status and bounded logs exist. TST2: no public isolation/concurrency/security tests were found. MNT3: simple locally, brittle across Docker/platform/image drift. COST4: efficient for one developer. PROD4: convenient local UX. SAAS1: not a production substrate. GEN2: useful only in development. FIN1: unsuitable for sensitive or regulated workloads. MIG2: easy to reproduce locally. DEP5: high dependence on Docker Desktop, Linux/amd64 emulation, a floating external image, and local CLI state.
notes: Reject only the production-security claim; the local-dev use is separately classified EXPERIMENT in the report.

pattern: Provider adapter seam across Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenRouter

pattern: Per-agent in-process promise queue and renderer event projection
current_project_counterpart: MASTER_OPERATING_PROMPT.md durable task states, interruption, retries, and multi-agent ownership requirements
recommended_action: Translate per-agent serialization into a durable distributed execution lane with leases, idempotency keys, generation fencing, persisted events, and a separate client projection.
future_stage: Stage 3 ADR then Stage 4 crash/replay spike
acceptance_test: Concurrent sends for one and many agents, worker death, lease expiry, provider switch, duplicate delivery, and replay preserve per-agent order with no shared-store lost update or duplicate external action.
score_rationale: COR2: one agent is serialized, but different agent queues load and rewrite one shared file and can lose updates; failures become assistant text. MOD4: queue, persistence, activity, and projection functions are visible. DUR1: all queue state is memory. MT1: no tenant identity. SEC2: little direct security enforcement. MP4: route selection is provider-independent at enqueue time. TP3: tool calls flow through but are not transactionally tied to turn state. OBS3: activity is visible, though synthesized by polling. TST2: no public concurrency/crash tests. MNT3: simple but unsuitable once distributed. COST5: very cheap locally. PROD4: responsive serialized turns fit UX. SAAS2: principle translates, implementation does not. GEN4: per-agent ownership is central. FIN2: finance requires durable, auditable execution. MIG2: concept is easy; productionization is not captured by this score. DEP3: event shapes depend on the shipped renderer.
notes: The 1.2-second activity delay and 250ms pulse are compatibility mechanisms, not runtime invariants.

pattern: Loopback routed MCP bridge and direct tool normalization
current_project_counterpart: MASTER_OPERATING_PROMPT.md tools, MCP, approval, audit, and external-state requirements
recommended_action: Build a tenant-aware capability gateway that normalizes tool schemas and results while preserving provider identity, capability version, authorization decision, idempotency, side-effect class, and audit receipt.
future_stage: Stage 3 ADR then Stage 4 capability-gateway spike
acceptance_test: Malformed schemas, unknown tools, stale capabilities, duplicate calls, denied scopes, approval expiry, provider disconnect, large results, and replay are handled deterministically with an immutable decision receipt.
score_rationale: COR3: protocol framing, size cap, tool mapping, and result normalization are clear, but side-effect classification is heuristic. MOD4: the bridge isolates provider protocol differences. DUR1: discovery and routing state are memory-only. MT1: no tenant, actor, or organization context. pattern: Turn- and resource-scoped local approval controller

recommended_action: Preserve scope epochs, expiry, deduplicated prompts, remembered refusal, resource binding, and completion retirement; add tenant/org policy, actor identity, durable decisions, risk classes, and external-state receipts.

acceptance_test: Old approvals cannot authorize a new turn, target, tenant, tool, or widened action; crash/restart preserves denials and settled decisions; standing permissions obey organization ceilings and all actions produce readback-linked receipts.
score_rationale: COR4: scope keys, epochs, TTLs, retirement, and stale-task handling are detailed, with some state remaining process-local. MOD4: decision logic is separated from UI and execution. DUR2: approval files exist, but core controller maps are memory-only. MT1: no tenant/org/policy identity. SEC4: least-privilege concepts are strong, short of centralized policy and durable enforcement. MP5: model-agnostic. TP5: action/target/resource concepts generalize across tools. OBS4: created/settled events and refusal memory are inspectable. TST4: deterministic clock/random/ports make it testable, though public regression coverage is limited. pattern: Bounded group, agent-to-agent, channel, and automation orchestration

recommended_action: Define durable message envelopes and execution ownership with sender/tenant identity, sequence, dedupe key, delivery status, visibility scope, cancellation, deadline, policy, and causal links; keep bounded group rounds and automation coalescing.

score_rationale: COR3: group caps, mention routing, run IDs, and bounded history are explicit, but A2A queues and overlap guards are memory-only and channel addresses are thin. MOD4: group, messaging, channel, schedule, and store modules are separated. DUR2: files preserve some definitions/runs; delivery ownership is not durable. MT1: no complete tenant/org authorization. pattern: Evidence-anchor catalogs, immutable fingerprints, component/symbol manifests, and explicit closure blockers
current_project_counterpart: FILE_MANIFEST.json; SOURCE_LEDGER.csv; task registry, handoffs, verifier artifacts, checkpoints, and planned benchmark manifests
recommended_action: Add schema-versioned claim-to-evidence manifests, live artifact hashes, interface inventories, closure status, negative boundaries, and explicit promotion blockers to research, architecture, benchmark, and release artifacts.
future_stage: Immediate future governance/harness proposal; adoption only through a registered task
acceptance_test: Every consequential claim resolves to an immutable digest or authoritative record; missing, changed, orphaned, or forbidden evidence fails validation; blocked closure cannot be promoted by a passing build alone.
score_rationale: COR5: exact artifacts, offsets, digests, and negative boundaries sharply constrain unsupported claims. MOD4: separate manifests cover distinct evidence classes, though some are very large. DUR5: immutable fingerprints and retained blockers survive narrative drift. MT3: not a runtime tenancy pattern, but manifests can carry tenant-safe provenance. SEC4: forbidden-file and secret/reconstructed boundaries improve release safety; rights review remains external. MP5 and TP5: the method is provider/tool neutral. OBS5: evidence state is highly inspectable. TST5: manifests are machine-verifiable and support drift tests. MNT4: schema/versioning helps, but huge generated audits need tooling. COST4: generation costs are modest relative to prevented regressions. PROD4: indirectly improves trust. SAAS5: directly useful for release certification. GEN5 and FIN5: universal; finance requires this level of provenance. MIG3: moderate schema/tooling work. DEP1: low dependency risk.
notes: Primary governance is stronger on independent review; external harness is stronger on machine-linked artifact identity.

pattern: Deterministic packaging, exact-anchor transforms, runtime verification, and clean-history publication check
current_project_counterpart: Future release gates and architecture drift detection are required but not yet implemented
recommended_action: Adopt deterministic transforms, output manifests, forbidden-artifact checks, clean-source publication, and release attestation; do not carry the minified renderer patch or Electron-specific packaging path.
acceptance_test: Two clean builds from the same inputs produce identical declared artifacts or documented nondeterminism; CI rejects forbidden files, stale generated manifests, missing source maps policy, dirty/untracked release inputs, and unverifiable signatures.
score_rationale: COR4: exact-once anchors and post-build verification fail loudly, though equivalence still depends on scoped rules. MOD4: build, patch, package, verify, and publication phases are separated. DUR4: hashes and manifests preserve build identity. MT2: packaging is not tenant-aware. SEC3: forbidden artifacts, checksum, signature, and updater guards help; known advisories and ad-hoc signing remain. MP3 and TP3: general build principles transfer, product details do not. OBS4: emitted manifests and diagnostics are strong. TST4: focused checks exist, but macOS packaging/smoke are not run by the Linux CI workflow. MNT3: exact minified anchors are brittle. COST3: verification adds build time. PROD3: important for distribution, not core behavior. SAAS2: only the release-harness subset translates. GEN3 and FIN2: shared release value, limited direct product value. MIG4: nontrivial CI/release work. DEP5: current implementation depends heavily on Electron, one pinned app, macOS tools, and shipped bundles.
notes: The publication check proves the committed HEAD archive is lossless; it does not certify a dirty working tree or release provenance by itself.

pattern: Current Electron main/preload/renderer and secret bridge as a SaaS security blueprint
current_project_counterpart: SECURITY.md and Stage 3 threat-model requirements; R-003, R-004, R-009
recommended_action: Do not translate the broad trusted-renderer bridge, raw secret reveal, unsandboxed windows, or local account-slot model into the SaaS control plane; retain only narrowly scoped validation and OS-vault lessons.
acceptance_test: Renderer compromise cannot reveal raw credentials, install arbitrary capabilities, widen policy, or reach another tenant; every privileged operation is server-authorized, capability-scoped, audited, rate-limited, and independently revocable.
score_rationale: COR3: trusted top-frame checks and navigation denial reduce accidental misuse, but broad object payloads weaken enforcement. MOD3: main/preload separation exists, yet the bridge exposes a very large privileged surface. DUR3: encrypted stores and migrations are thoughtful. MT1: account slot is not a tenant/RBAC model. SEC2: context isolation and OS encryption help, but sandbox false, global no-sandbox, webviewTag, broad secret reveal, and local credential reuse are high risk. MP3: provider secrets are exposed through one bridge. TP4: many tool surfaces are reachable. OBS4: desktop telemetry is extensive. TST3: some guards are tested, not a full privilege matrix. MNT3: large bridge and hand-wired methods drift easily. COST3: desktop local trust is operationally cheap. PROD4: supports a rich desktop UX. SAAS1: wrong trust model. GEN2 and FIN1: insufficient for sensitive shared service use. MIG5: replacing it requires a real identity/policy plane. DEP5: tightly Electron and local-session dependent.
notes: Sound subpatterns are listed separately in the report; rejection targets the blueprint as a whole.

acceptance_test: A Finance pack installs without modifying generic runtime code; signatures, compatibility, policy, tool capabilities, data entitlements, migrations, rollback, and evaluation pack all verify before activation.
score_rationale: COR3: origin and enablement rules are clear, but helper scripts and live file imports are not a secure package contract. MOD4: user, managed, plugin, and automation sources converge on one view. DUR3: file stores and migration preserve definitions. MT1: no tenant package policy. SEC2: helper scripts and imported local files need signing, sandboxing, and capability review. MP4: instruction packs are model-neutral. TP5: tools and helper assets can extend behavior. OBS3: origin fields are visible, but no cryptographic attestation. TST3: parsers/stores are testable; package conformance is absent. MNT4: unified records avoid duplicate vertical runtimes. COST5: extension packs reuse the core efficiently. PROD5: supports skills and editions. SAAS3: principle translates with a registry and policy plane. GEN5 and FIN5: ideal shared-core boundary. MIG3: moderate package/schema work. DEP2: principle is portable.
notes: This is the best external clue for D-014, but its file loading must not be copied.

pattern: Structured lifecycle telemetry, privacy tiers, request lineage, and drop accounting
current_project_counterpart: MASTER_OPERATING_PROMPT.md audit, observability, metering, privacy, and external verification requirements
recommended_action: Define a tenant-safe event envelope with schema version, actor/agent/task/turn/tool lineage, privacy class, evidence links, dropped-event accounting, and immutable audit/export separation.
acceptance_test: Every turn and consequential tool call can be reconstructed from redacted traces and durable audit receipts; privacy policy changes purge or reclassify buffered data; deliberate drop and backpressure tests account for every missing event.
score_rationale: COR4: explicit event names, lineage, privacy tiers, and drop reasons reduce ambiguity; not every event payload is strongly typed. MOD4: shared taxonomy and sinks are separated. DUR3: spill/replay concepts exist, but not all telemetry is durable audit. MT2: machine/account tags exist without complete tenant policy. SEC3: privacy gating and scrubbing help; identifiers and broad metadata still need minimization. MP4 and TP4: taxonomy spans providers and tools. OBS5: very broad lifecycle coverage. TST4: deterministic projections and drop cases are testable, with limited public tests. MNT4: centralized names aid evolution. COST3: rich telemetry has storage/processing cost. PROD4: improves support and trust. SAAS4: strong translation after tenancy and retention controls. GEN5 and FIN5: both benefit; finance needs audit-grade separation from telemetry. MIG3: moderate schema/pipeline work. DEP3: current sinks include Sentry/OTLP and reconstructed backend assumptions.
notes: Telemetry is not evidence of external completion; link it to independent readback receipts.

pattern: Desktop updater state machine and signed/checksummed artifact application
current_project_counterpart: Future release gates only; no desktop-client decision
recommended_action: Retain as future desktop-client reference only; for SaaS, translate the relevant invariant into signed release manifests, staged rollout, health gates, rollback, and deployment attestation.
future_stage: Post-architecture or only if a desktop client is selected
acceptance_test: A signed release is checksum-verified, policy-gated, staged, health-checked, rollback-capable, and traceable to source/build evidence; no client updater code is adopted before a client architecture decision.
score_rationale: COR4: explicit check/download/stage/ready/apply states, track gates, aborts, checksum, and Windows signature checks are strong. MOD4: feed, download, apply, gate, and wiring are separate. DUR4: staged markers and supersession tracking survive lifecycle transitions. MT1: desktop machine scope only. SEC4: checksum and signature validation are sound, though reconstructed packages deliberately disable upstream updates and use ad-hoc signing. MP1 and TP2: largely unrelated to model/tool portability. OBS4: check/outcome/apply telemetry is explicit. TST4: state machine is injectable; public packaging CI is incomplete. MNT4: named states and ports aid change. COST3: update infrastructure has moderate cost. PROD3: valuable only if desktop distribution is chosen. SAAS1: not the SaaS deployment model. GEN2 and FIN1: limited direct impact. MIG5: high if no desktop client exists. DEP5: Squirrel, Electron, platform installers, and upstream compatibility dominate.
notes: Deferral is not a recommendation to adopt Electron or a desktop updater.
